subtitle: Five ideas about public life, tested on three islands with the same toolkit.

themes.title: Roads are made for movement, not staying

cells.why: 64% of pedestrians were commuting; no children played in the street.
89% of people were moving through, 11% staying.
26% of people stopped, and 268 children were counted in the street.
87% walked in shade by evening, and more people walked.
12 of 14 walked in shade with 30% of the street shaded. Small counts.
90% walked in shade by evening; 3.6 times as many walkers.
Open frontage, heavy traffic: people pass through and do not stay.
Fewest doors, best lingering: low traffic lets people stay.
Most open edges, lowest lingering: six-lane roads push people off.

themes.title: Density is not the problem, poor design is

cells.why: 10 of 31 dense plots score good; all 5 that are not dense score poor.
91% of dense plots score poor, and 86% of the rest.
8 plots of one building type, all at one point.
13% of street users overall, but 51.9% in Area 03.
51 pedestrians in all: shares swing on a handful of people.
4.3% of users; the busiest areas are the least conflicted.

tasksTitle: What each masterplan has to answer
tasksSubtitle: The findings, turned into tasks. Chapter 03 takes them up island by island.

tasks: Give people reasons and places to stop. The streets move them and do not hold them.
Shade the streets people have to walk, not only the ones they choose.
Take vehicles off the places where people on foot are outnumbered, as in Area 03.
Raise housing quality by design. Lowering density would not do it.
Bring everyday activity to the frontage, so the streets are more than routes.
Keep traffic low. That is what lets walking and staying overlap here.
Lift housing quality across the area: it is low whatever the density.
Give the industrial block the few active spots the rest of the island has.
Bring life out from the sheltered interior to the edges, where six-lane roads now push it away.
Add shade along the routes: three times as many people walk when they are shaded.
Break the single building type with variety and a human scale.
Keep parked vehicles at the edges, where they already do least harm.

sources: Sections 2.3 to 2.7. A grey dot means the island had nothing to compare.
note: The site diagnosis in 2.1 lists what is wrong in each area. These tasks add what the five themes showed.
